hints: Start with the ideal gas equation and remember how moles links mass to $M_r$.
Replace $n$ in $pV = nRT$ with $n = m / M_r$ to get $pV = (m/M_r)RT$.
Rearrange to make $M_r$ the subject by getting it on top on its own, then check which fraction has $mRT$ on top and $pV$ below.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two key equations**

Think like a chemist. Gases are described by one equation, and moles by another. Put them together.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$pV = nRT \quad \text{and} \quad n = \frac{m}{M_r}$$

**Combine them into one equation**

Substitute the moles expression into the gas equation. This links the measured $p$, $V$, $T$ and mass $m$ directly to $M_r$.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$pV = \left(\frac{m}{M_r}\right)RT$$

**Rearrange to make $M_r$ the subject**

Multiply both sides by $M_r$ to remove it from the denominator, then divide both sides by $pV$ to isolate it.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$pV \times M_r = mRT \quad \text{so} \quad M_r = \frac{mRT}{pV}$$

options.A: This is the correct rearrangement. From $pV = (m/M_r)RT$, multiplying by $M_r$ and dividing by $pV$ gives $M_r = mRT/pV$. The units also work, mass on top gives a molar mass.
options.B: This multiplies by $RT$ instead of dividing. If you just put everything together as $pVRT/m$ without rearranging properly, you get this. Check: $pV$ must end up in the denominator when you isolate $M_r$.
options.C: This has $pV$ on top and $RT$ below, which is upside down. It comes from swapping numerator and denominator when rearranging $pV = (m/M_r)RT$. Remember $M_r$ starts in the denominator, so $pV$ must move to the denominator.
options.D: This is the reciprocal, $1/M_r$. It equals $pV/mRT$. This is the classic trap of stopping one step too early and making $1/M_r$ the subject instead of $M_r$ itself.
